content: The World Health Organization (WHO) defines high-quality health services as those that are effective, safe, and people-centered. Effectiveness refers to the provision of evidence-based healthcare services to individuals who need them. Safety involves avoiding harm to patients for whom the care is intended. People-centered care ensures that services are tailored to individual preferences, needs, and values. To achieve the benefits of high-quality healthcare, services must also be timely, equitable, integrated, and efficient. Timeliness involves reducing waiting times and harmful delays for both patients and providers. Equity ensures that the quality of care does not vary based on factors such as age, sex, gender, race, ethnicity, geographical location, religion, socioeconomic status, or political affiliation. Integration refers to the coordination of care across different levels and providers, ensuring the availability of a comprehensive range of health services throughout the life course. Efficiency focuses on maximizing the benefits of available resources while minimizing waste. High-quality HIV services require the reliable delivery of people-centered clinical care across various community and facility settings. These services should be integrated with other health services, such as maternal, newborn, and child health services, at national, subnational, district, and facility levels. The delivery of such services depends on the strength of the underlying health system, which includes optimized management, adequate funding, skilled human resources, robust information systems, and the procurement of high-quality pharmaceuticals, devices, and laboratory supplies. National HIV programs must ensure quality management through appropriate structures, functions, and processes to support the delivery of high-quality HIV services. Quality management encompasses all activities within the overall management function that determine quality policies, objectives, and responsibilities. These are implemented through quality planning, quality assurance, and quality improvement. Quality planning involves setting overall quality objectives, identifying priority indicators, establishing governance and organizational structures, selecting health service personnel, allocating resources, monitoring and evaluating performance, and designing and overseeing quality improvement and assurance initiatives. Quality assurance refers to systematic assessment and monitoring activities aimed at ensuring that services meet established quality standards. This includes measuring performance against standards, conducting external evaluations (e.g., accreditation), communicating standards to users, and monitoring compliance with these standards. Examples in HIV programs include site-level assessments, quality assurance checklists for rapid HIV tests, and supportive supervision. Quality improvement is a methodical approach designed to continuously enhance performance as part of routine processes. It is typically applied by health facility teams within national quality improvement programs. This involves testing changes in program services, measuring the effects of these changes, and using data to address gaps in clinical performance and health outcomes over time. National quality policies and strategies are organized efforts by countries to promote and plan for improving the quality of care across the health system. These efforts support leadership and ownership of high-quality HIV initiatives by national health authorities, ensuring integration with broader national health planning and other disease-specific programs. The WHO Handbook for National Quality Policy and Strategy outlines a non-prescriptive approach to developing policies and strategies to support high-quality health programs and services. This approach focuses on eight interdependent elements that help countries establish their national direction on quality of care. Quality management strategies and frameworks, including those aimed at reducing stigma and discrimination, involve activities at multiple levels of the health system. These activities extend beyond clinical audits and routine quality assessments to include community-based monitoring. Effective quality management strategies require a systemic understanding of the complexity of HIV care, recognizing that changes in one aspect of the system may have unintended consequences elsewhere. Quality assurance in healthcare delivery involves systematic assessment and monitoring to ensure that services meet stated quality requirements. National quality assurance systems typically include organizations and processes external to healthcare providers, such as standard-setting bodies, professional licensing boards, and external evaluation programs. HIV programs should consider mechanisms for setting appropriate standards, monitoring service quality, and aligning with broader health system approaches to assurance while building accountability into program management. Quality improvement requires a systematic approach to identifying gaps in service delivery, exploring root causes, and designing and implementing contextually appropriate solutions. This process involves robust data collection, reporting, and the use of standardized indicators. Interoperable information systems facilitate the measurement of service quality, address knowledge gaps, and communicate findings to end-users, such as district health management teams and facility-level quality committees. HIV programs often use quality improvement methods tailored to local capacity, resources, and available tools. Regardless of the chosen model, these programs aim to institutionalize a culture of quality improvement and build the necessary capacity for improvement across all levels. Quality improvement involves the collective efforts of various stakeholders to implement changes that enhance programs and systems, ultimately improving health outcomes. The WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services provide guidance on quality assurance for HIV testing. These guidelines include tools for setting and monitoring targets for HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations. Quality-related indicators and checklists are used to monitor performance and identify program bottlenecks, enabling the design of linked indicators to assess and improve service quality.
